newsitem.title: USA: Dlr rebounds from FOMC losses, closes higher in US.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rebounds from FOMC losses, closes higher in US.

text.p: The dollar rallied sharply against most major currencies on Wednesday as investors poured funds into bond markets with relatively high interest rates in Italy and the United States, dealers said.
U.S. bonds also rallied on investor relief after Federal Reserve policy makers declined to raise interest rates at a meeting Tuesday, driving up demand for dollars, dealers said.

The Italian lira rose against the Japanese yen and the German mark, helping the dollar rally against those currencies as well. Late in the session, the lira broke below 1000 to the mark, posting a two-year low at 996.

"Italy's bond market had a great day and that euphoria snowballed into the lira," said Jay Wertheimer, senior foreign exchange trader at Banco di Sicilia in New York. "After that we saw a wave a mark selling."
The dollar closed higher on Wednesday at 1.5165/75 marks from 1.5085/95 at the open and to 110.42/52 yen from 109.19/24.

Sterling fell to $1.56008/15 from $1.5625/35. The dollar also rose to 1.2410/20 Swiss francs from 1.2327/35, but stood little changed at Canadian $1.3661/66 from C$1.3665/70. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7910/15 from $0.7900/05.
Dealers also cited optimism that Italy might meet the strict financial requirements to qualify for a proposed single European currency for bolstering the lira.
"There's a feeling that Italy might get its act together in time to qualify," said Wertheimer.

Meanwhile, an International Monetary Fund report on Wednesday suggested that Germany may need to continue lowering domestic interest rates, even as U.S. interest rates seem certain to rise in coming months.
Higher interest rates tend to bolster the dollar by increasing the the returns on dollar-denominated assets.

"Interest rate differentials were a major reason for the day's action. It was a little selling of yen for lira early and it turned into marks for lira," said Greg Perman, chief dealer at Credit Commerciale de France.
The dollar began its rally overnight in Tokyo as investors abandoned the yen, dealers said.
By the start of U.S. trade the dollar had reclaimed nearly all of the ground it lost on Tuesday and extended its rally.
"The yen selling move started pretty much from the get-go in Tokyo. There was good interest to sell yen for dollars," said Thomas Arnold, chief dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.

Mutual fund investors initially sold the dollar on Tuesday afternoon on disappointment over the Fed's decision to leave interest rates steady, but as the U.S. currency recovered, many investors nervously bought it back.
"A lot of fund managers sold the dollar at poor levels Tuesday. Today they were reestablishing their positions," Arnold said.

Dollar/mark closed right on a key resistance point from last week, but dealers expected the greenback to continue testing that level in coming sessions. On dollar yen, 111 seems a possibility, dealers added.
"The buying in Japan really turned things around. The dollar has appreciated nicely," Wertheimer said.
